national.title: Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack
national.summary: Five people were killed in a wave of strikes which follow Ukraine's successful targeting of the Crimean Bridge.
national.body:
Russia has targeted bridges in Kyiv and killed eight during one of the largest air attacks of the war so far, days after Ukraine inflicted heavy damage on the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Two people were killed in Russian strikes on a railway station in the western city of Lviv.

Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro River, vital routes which people in Kyiv rely on to move around the city, with six deaths confirmed in the capital.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The three Kyiv bridges targeted overnight - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption created by retaliatory strikes on bridges earlier this week.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary".

He added that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was also damaged and seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault.

Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.

national.title: New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
national.summary: New York City officials are moving forward with plans to close Rikers, the city's main jail complex, after years of discussion. The jail has been plagued by assaults and inmate deaths.
national.body:
New York City officials have created a road map for how they'll close the jail complex on Rikers Island and move to smaller facilities within the boroughs. Mayor Zohran Mamdani closed the North Infirmary Command building, seen here, on Rikers earlier this year. Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR hide caption

New York City officials on Friday unveiled their plan to close the troubled jail complex on Rikers Island, the city's main pre-trial detention center, which has been plagued with reports of abuse and neglect for decades.

"It is long past time to close what's been a moral stain on our city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. "We cannot simply accept the old approaches to public safety just because they've always been done that way."

Rikers, which sits on a former garbage dump in the East River, has long been infamous for its dismal conditions – including crumbling infrastructure. Inmates have accused guards of excessive force, sexual assault and high rates of violence in multiple lawsuits.

Last year, a federal judge called the amount of violence at Rikers an "unconstitutional danger" for both the people held there and the staff.

Since 2022, more than 50 people have died in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. Almost all had been held at Rikers. People have been found unresponsive. They have died by suicide and been beaten to death. Federal court records say Rikers is "significantly more violent" than comparable jails.

But now, city officials say they finally have momentum to close the jail for good, and the newly released plan details how they intend to do that.

Empty cells at the Rikers Island jail complex in New York City on Nov. 18, 2026. The city's plan to close Rikers aims to transform the conditions inside the city's jails and lower their population. Nicky Quamina-Woo/NPR hide caption

national.title: The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
national.summary: A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences.
national.body:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham, left, and the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen, right, attend a bilateral meeting during the European Political Community (EPC) summit in Dublin, Ireland, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA via AP hide caption

BRUSSELS — A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.

Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.

Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.

"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.

Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.

FILE - A Union flag waves behind a European Union flag, outside the Houses of Parliament, in London, Wednesday, Oct. 19, 2022. Alberto Pezzali/AP hide caption

Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be "a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security."

national.body: Houthi authorities accused Saudi forces on Friday of attacking a civilian boat and killing 19 people, after Yemen's dormant civil war reignited. Conflict flared up in July after years of relative calm, pitting the internationally recognized government, backed by Saudi Arabia, against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi on Friday condemned the "horrific massacre committed by the Saudi enemy planes, which targeted a civilian boat carrying more than 25 displaced persons ... which resulted in the martyrdom of 19 civilians and left 4 others wounded." "Targeting civilians and displaced persons constitutes a full-fledged war crime and a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law and human rights," Alasbahi added. Eight children and six women were among the dead, according to the Houthis' Almasirah television channel. The boat was travelling from Ras al-Ara to Hays in the country's south, Alasbahi said on X. Houthi media, including Ansarollah and the Saba news agency reported on Friday that Saudi planes had struck Yemen's capital, Sanaa. They also launched attacks on Taiz, in the country's southwest, according to Ansarollah.

Its shares were priced at $83 each, well above the targeted range of $70 to $78 apiece, suggesting strong investor demand.That came to pass as its price quickly surged above $115 once trading began. Shares later lost some of their early gains and wound up at $97.17 — still 17.1% higher.The IPO was the largest in U.S. history, surpassing SpaceX's $75 billion public offering in June.The IPO also turned many Anthropic employees into instant millionaires. The typical worker at the company could be worth more than $40 million after the initial stock sale, CNBC reported, citing regulatory filings and investors. national.summary: Significant flooding devastated some South Florida communities this week.
national.body: South Florida communities are reeling in the aftermath of widespread flooding that forced evacuations and school closures this week.Rain lashed coastal areas east of Orlando, dumping as much as eight inches there by early Thursday afternoon. In the city of Palm Bay, near Cape Canaveral, officials announced a mix of mandatory and voluntary evacuations for different neighborhoods and offered to transport residents away from their homes by boat.Parts of Florida's Broward County, which includes Fort Lauderdale and the nearby coastal city of Hollywood, received more than 17 inches of rain, and up to a foot of rain fell in other areas. Photos and video footage show neighborhoods inundated, with residential properties and vehicles partially submerged in water.CBS News Miami reported that floodwaters were receding across South Florida late on Thursday. But heavy rains and flash flooding were expected to continued through Friday as the storms moved north, possibly toward the Carolinas and the mid-Atlantic into the weekend, the National Weather Service said.Fort Lauderdale Fire Rescue shared multiple videos to social media that captured its crew members either driving or wading on foot through knee-high waters. In several of them, rescuers were seen collecting debris and approaching vehicles that had become stranded on flooded roads.One video, shared by X user Sruly Meyer, showed floodwaters rushing over a Hollywood street where his Uber was driving. The water appeared to create small waves that lapped against tree trunks and inched up the surrounding driveways. "Insane flooding. Uber to airport," Meyer captioned the video. national.title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
national.summary: The scheme is expected to be approved at Friday's UK-EU summit, with new deals on food trade and carbon emissions also on the table.
national.body:
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

national.title: Beloved hippo Fiona dies days after swallowing hat
national.summary: Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely and rose to global fame, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday.
national.body: Fiona the hippo, who survived being born prematurely almost a decade ago, and whose story captured hearts around the world, has died, the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced Thursday. "We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a news release. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, had ingested a knit hat that ended up in her enclosure by accident last week, the zoo said, and despite the team's efforts to get it out of her system, "it was ultimately too much to overcome."A Cincinnati Zoo spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that the hat Fiona swallowed had been tossed in the air by a zoo visitor, then catapulted it into the enclosure by a ceiling fan."Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said. "She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many."Before Fiona's death, veterinarians closely monitored her health, turning to an unconventional method to try to help her pass the blockage by borrowing a vibration plate from a horse farm. They had Fiona stand on the device several times a day, hoping the vibrations would help move the material through her digestive system.Fiona would have been 10 years old this January. Her birth in 2017 drew the attention of millions on social media after she was born prematurely, weighing just 29 pounds, far below the typical 55–120 pounds for a newborn Nile hippo. Fiona was the first Nile hippo born at the zoo in 75 years. To support baby Fiona, zoo staffers worked around the clock to care for her, including bottle-feeding her and helping her learn to swim. In August 2022, Fiona's little brother, Fritz, was born at the Cincinnati Zoo. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine called Fiona "a true icon" of the zoo, saying in a social media post that she "captured the hearts of Ohioans and those around the world, bringing joy to millions." national.title: Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
national.summary: Nigeria's proposed reform follows years of calls from psychiatrists and a parallel Senate bill.
national.body:
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.

The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.

It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.

Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.

The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.

It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.

He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.

He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.

national.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
national.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
national.body:
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.

A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.

"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.

"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."

Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.

Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.

In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.

Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.

national.title: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
national.summary: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.
national.body:
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.

Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.

Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.

Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.

Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.

national.title: DOJ moves to dismiss lawsuit over Alaska Senate race
national.summary: The Trump administration is moving to effectively drop its legal challenge to Democrat Mary Peltola's win in Alaska's Senate race.
national.body: The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot. Earlier this month, a federal judge in Alaska threw out the Trump administration's lawsuit.Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground." "The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of 'determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,'" Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote in the filing.That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. national.summary: Texas execution takes over an hour amid complications.
national.body: Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital. And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times, and asked God to take him away from the pain. Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately.The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered. Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. national.body:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday , after a 13-year wait.

The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas .

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history .

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop , which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

national.title: US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume
national.summary: The Army has delayed the controlled explosion of unstable lead azide in eastern Iowa to Monday after concerns from residents and lawmakers.
national.body:
The US Army is set to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosive material in Middletown, Iowa, and have urged locals to vacate the area or stay indoors for their safety.

The detonations will result in an air plume that could send toxic dust, containing lead particles, over eastern Iowa and into neighbouring Illinois, with the potential for contaminants to settle on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, the army said.

The two controlled explosions will be powerful enough that they could damage buildings and shatter windows nearby.

On Thursday, environmental groups sued in an effort to stop the detonations, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon local time (1800 BST) on Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown - a community of about 360 people about four hours west of Chicago, Illinois.

The plant produces medium- and large-calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.

On Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle delayed the detonation to Monday, saying that "public safety is the Army's top priority".

The planned detonation will be "the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material", he said on X.

national.body: A 2-year-old who went missing was found safe, if not a little cold, by a volunteer after spending seven hours alone in the Arizona desert.Jay Stewart was overcome with emotion during a news conference as he recalled the moment he found her curled up under a bush just after midnight on Wednesday."To find that little scared child, the way she popped out of that bush, it was, I'll never forget it as long as I live," he said.Stewart responded to a post from the Pinal County sheriff pleading for help after Vella Campillo, wearing only a diaper, wandered out of her yard outside Eloy, Arizona, just before sunset Tuesday. The sheriff's office said in a statement the search involved more than 100 people on foot."We used drones, helicopters, everything that we could throw at it," Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple said. "We forget in the wintertime that very remote areas like this can get extremely cold very fast. And she's a small body producing very little heat. So the drones with the heat signatures could not pick up anything."Stewart had been searching on foot for three hours when he spotted her about a mile and a half from her house. He said in a video posted to the sheriff's office's Facebook page that he was calling the little girl's name when he heard her yell, so he shined his flashlight on a bush, "and she popped up. It was a life-changing moment.""I grabbed her and picked her up and then she was, like, clinging to me so tight, so tight," he said at the news conference.He tucked the toddler inside his jacket. Thankfully, she was uninjured."I know you've been asked this 1,000 times, whether you feel you're a hero, and you say you're not, but I'm here to tell you that, when you watch the body camera footage, it's obvious that you're that little girl's hero," Teeple said in the social media video.Stewart said at the news conference, "The scariest thing for parents is to lose a child. I can't imagine what they were going through. They thanked me profusely, of course, but they didn't need to thank me. It's what we do."

national.summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
national.body:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

national.title: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
national.summary: Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary is among the big investors looking to Canada as a data centre development destination, while his US project faces local opposition.
national.body:
As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.

"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.

While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.

Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.

"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.

"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."

Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.

At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.

national.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis
national.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in the key city of Taiz, cut off from the outside world for weeks.
national.body:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

national.title: Do you need a measles booster shot now that the U.S. has lost its elimination status?
national.summary: The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress.
national.body:
Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?

"Most people are protected without getting a booster shot" because they've either been vaccinated or had measles as kids, said Dr. Richard Martinello at Yale School of Medicine.

The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress. Last year, Canada lost its measles-elimination designation.

Doctors say getting two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is the best way to protect against one of the most contagious viruses in the world. The vaccine usually protects people for life, as does having had the disease. Americans born before 1957 are considered to have "presumptive evidence" of immunity because almost everyone back then got measles during childhood.

But doctors say certain people should consider getting boosters.

One group is healthcare workers born before 1957 without proof of immunity. They're more likely than the general public to come in contact with people who have measles, so they may get it or even spread it to vulnerable patients.

Adults vaccinated between 1963 and 1967 also might want to think about boosters. During those years, some children received an inactivated vaccine that uses a killed version of the virus, which was less effective than the current vaccine containing live, weakened virus. Doctors said people who know they got the inactivated vaccine or aren't sure should get at least one dose of the live MMR vaccine. One dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, while two doses are 97% protective.

Until 1989, only a single dose was standard. Now the recommendation is for adults to have at least one documented dose of MMR. Two doses are recommended for certain people in high-risk groups who don't have other evidence of immunity.

national.title: FCC votes to allow state prisons to jam signals from contraband cellphones
national.summary: The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday acted to allow state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cellphones smuggled to inmates as the federal government cracks down on devices that authorities say are the No. 1 security threat in the nation's correctional facilities.
national.body:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday acted to allow state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cellphones smuggled to inmates as the federal government cracks down on devices that authorities say are the No. 1 security threat in the nation's correctional facilities.

The vote was unanimous among the commissioners meeting in Washington.

State prison officials for years have sought the right to jam, arguing that blocking the signals of contraband phones would halt inmates' ability to use the devices to run drug rings, coordinate prison riots and even order acts of violence such as attacks on guards.

Under the new rule, prisons are not required to use the jamming technology, they must conduct multiple tests to make sure cell signals outside prisons are not affected and they have to notify officials if the jamming devices are moved.

Commissioner Anna Gomez, who ultimately voted for the measure on what she called a "critical" issue, expressed concern for "potential unintended consequences" that could come if jamming zones were improperly calibrated in ways that accidentally disrupted home security systems or blocked emergency response calls.

"I want to make sure that we don't harm public safety in the name of helping public safety," she said. Gomez is the lone Democrat on the panel.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who spoke in favor of the measure, visited this week with officials in South Carolina, whose prison directors have led efforts to obtain permission to jam.

"This itself is not going to be a silver bullet, but I think it's time that we stop denying this tool to state and local officials," Carr said before the vote.

national.title: Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
national.summary: Rose, who died in 2024, was given a lifetime ban from the sport for betting on games but was reinstated last year.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.

Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.

The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.

Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".

In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.

According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".

The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.

national.title: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
national.summary: Fiona, who became an internet star after her premature birth in 2017, "fought until she couldn’t anymore", the zoo says.
national.body:
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.

"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.

Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and required emergency care.

The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.

"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

national.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
national.summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
national.body:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

TURIN, Italy (AP) -- U.S. Open finalist Ben Shelton did his part. Then he got some help from top-ranked Alexander Zverev to advance at the ATP Finals.

Shelton twice aced his way out of trouble in the first-set tiebreaker and beat Rafael Jodar 7-6 (8), 7-5 on Thursday.

When Zverev beat Arthur Fils 6-4, 7-6 (6) later in the final match of the group, Shelton was secured a spot in the semifinals of the elite event for the season’s top eight players.

Shelton will face Carlos Alcaraz in the semifinals in another rematch of their U.S. Open quarterfinal that ended at 3:33 a.m.

While Shelton won that five-set clash in New York, Alcaraz recently got revenge in the Paris Masters final.

Alcaraz has an injury concern, though, after getting his left thigh strapped during a victory over Daniil Medvedev on Wednesday; and plays Flavio Cobolli in his final group match on Friday.

Zverev, who had already advanced and finished group play with a perfect three wins, will face either Medvedev or Frances Tiafoe -- who play Friday to determine the last semifinalist.

Zverev appeared to have an issue during the tiebreaker. He said afterward the problem is his ankle.

local.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Rasmus Dahlin and Beck Malenstyn scored 25 seconds apart in the first period to chase Logan Thompson, and the Buffalo Sabres sent Washington to its fourth straight loss, beating the Capitals 6-3 on Thursday night.

Jack Quinn scored twice -- once into an empty net -- and Zach Benson and Tage Thompson also scored for the Sabres. Buffalo converted on five of its 13 shots in the first two periods. Alex Tuch, Ryan Leonard and Boone Jenner scored Washington, which has fallen to .500 after entering the season with lofty expectations.

Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington’s career lead in assists with his 763rd.

The Capitals have allowed at least five goals in four straight games and six of their last eight. On Wednesday it took them only two periods to do so. Thompson allowed three goals on five shots before being yanked in favor of Charlie Lindgren.

It was the second time in his last six starts Thompson was pulled early.

After Quinn opened the scoring, Dahlin entered the zone on a power play, and when Thompson overplayed him a bit to the near post, the Buffalo defenseman swooped behind the net and wrapped the puck into the vacated other side.

Tuch scored again against his former team. He had two goals against Buffalo, including the winner in overtime, in a game last month.

It was 4-1 after one Thursday, and Tage Thompson scored on the power play near the end of the second. Leonard scored to cap a dominant stretch on the power play for Washington in the third, then Jenner poked the puck in with 10:16 remaining after Buffalo goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen seemed unaware it was loose.

local.title: Other voices: Air traffic system needs reforms
local.summary: And you thought flying in America couldn’t get worse. Then on Friday more than 12,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered an extraordinary nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Was there a terrorist threat? Cyber-attack? No, the cause appears to
local.body:
And you thought flying in America couldn't get worse. Then on Friday more than 12,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered an extraordinary nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Was there a terrorist threat? Cyber-attack? No, the cause appears to have been routine government failure.

Friday's fiasco, which disrupted millions of travel plans, laid bare the myriad dysfunctions of America's government-run air-traffic control system that have led to repeated system failures and delays. Flyers were left stranded for hours as the FAA tried to diagnose and fix the problem, which officials eventually tied to a new router at a facility in Arkansas.

According to FAA officials, the router along with another one in Texas flooded its communications system with data. It's far from reassuring that one or two malfunctioning devices can take down continental air traffic. Or that the Sherlock Holmeses at the FAA still aren't sure exactly what went wrong.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed either a faulty device or "incompetence" by the contractor L3Harris Technologies that had installed it. HPE, the router manufacturer, said its hardware "did not fail." While Mr. Duffy claimed the government hasn't found evidence of nefarious causes, it's understandable to wonder given that adversaries are stepping up cyberattacks across the U.S. economy and government.

As is their habit, politicians rushed to capitalize on the public misery. Democrats blamed the Administration's new SMART system, which uses AI to analyze airline schedules, weather, airspace conditions, among other things, to prevent flight conflicts that cause delays. There's no evidence the AI system contributed to Friday's problems.

Mr. Duffy on Thursday called for $30 billion in more funding, on top of the $12.5 billion Republicans appropriated in last year's tax bill. After Friday's failure, he raised the demand to $50 billion. But throwing more money at an unaccountable agency will at best be a temporary fix and will reward dysfunction.

In 2003 Congress directed the FAA to modernize America's aging air-traffic system, yet the Government Accountability Office reported in September that the FAA doesn't plan to complete the first phase of upgrades until December 2028. That's a quarter-century.

The GAO also said the FAA lacks a reliable estimate for when the second phase will be done and how much the entire project will cost. This is government incompetence across several administrations at a California bullet-train-to-nowhere level. Criticism from Pete Buttigieg, the Biden transportation secretary, is especially laughable given his obvious failure to improve things over four years in the job. And he apparently wants to run for President again.

local.summary: When Ty Harper took over as head coach at Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton a season ago, he arrived in Mayville with a stable of receiving options at his disposal. local.body:
When Ty Harper took over as head coach at Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton a season ago, he arrived in Mayville with a stable of receiving options at his disposal.

Devin Hewes would end up with 57 catches for 708 yards and six touchdowns and tight end Asher Olson had 39 catches for 642 yards and nine touchdowns while Nick Jacobson, a returning New York State Sportswriters Association Class C second-team all-star, battled injuries throughout the season.

A year later those three, in addition to third-leading receiver Carson Fairbank, were lost to graduation and the Eagles were left wondering who would fill the void.

"There was concern across the board. Anytime you have to replace nine guys on offense, that's a pretty big task," Harper said Tuesday evening. "When you couple having to replace all of those talented players with the fact that you're interjecting a sophomore into the most important position on the field. I would say there was probably some anxiety coming into the season."

Juniors Aiden Woodis and Ian Kindermann have answered the call, giving first-year sophomore starting quarterback Josh Swan reliable options in the passing game.

The aerial attack, which came through in two key instances a week ago, will likely be needed again at noon Saturday when Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton takes on Hornell/Arkport-Canaseraga in the Class C Far West Regional at SUNY Brockport's Bob Boozer Field at Eunice Kennedy Shriver Stadium.

Woodis has been more of a chain mover for the Eagles. He has 27 receptions for 288 yards and two scores on the year.

"He just made plays all the time. You get to see these guys in practice every day. The competitors really kind of separate themselves. You can tell when kids are competing all the time. Aiden just kind of had that characteristic from Day 1 last year in practice. We have jayvee in burgundy and varsity in navy; Aiden spent maybe five minutes in a red jersey before we told him to go put a navy jersey on," Harper said. "Aiden has been hampered by that knee injury from the state semifinals last year. He's going to need surgery at some point to repair his knee. He's gutting it out. To people who aren't there every day it might look like production is down, but he's doing a lot for us and is not close to 100%."

local.title: Ninety percent is not diversity of thought
local.summary: From previous years, you, faithful reader of this column, know what has happened. An organization legally separate from Chautauqua Institution and headquartered outside of the institution annually invites a speaker to the institution. More than 90 percent of the speakers over the years have been lib
local.body:
From previous years, you, faithful reader of this column, know what has happened. An organization legally separate from Chautauqua Institution and headquartered outside of the institution annually invites a speaker to the institution. More than 90 percent of the speakers over the years have been liberals.

Guess what? That's right. The organization invited another liberal in 2026.

Please don't misunderstand: The organization has every right to be as liberal as it wants to be. At its Chautauqua events, it has no obligation ever to give a non-liberal the time of day, much less invite a non-liberal to stand on its podium or behind its lectern.

You've read here about the organization's Chautauqua speakers in recent years.

The 2023 speaker disagreed with the Supreme Court's holding that race-based college and university admissions violate the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

The 2024 speaker--whom Chautauqua Institution has invited to give a morning-amphitheater lecture in 2027--described non-liberal high-court results with words such as "madness," "hubris," "a lack of humility," "wildly disruptive," "outlandish," and "audacious."

The 2025 speaker said a 2000 high-court opinion was "the first time really that the Supreme Court made a decision that was just impossible to justify on the basis of its pre-existing law." Thus, the speaker believes (1) Dred Scott v. Sandford, the 1857 decision creating a right to own slaves where no such right had existed, and (2) Plessy v. Ferguson, the 1896 decision upholding racially-segregated public accommodations, were possible for the Supreme Court "to justify on the basis of its pre-existing law."

Then came 2026, when the speaker was a veteran of two investigations of President Trump 45. Although that doesn't reveal the speaker's perspective, those hoping for diversity of thought could have suspected they were in for disappointment when the speaker prefaced thoughts on three topics with this: "It's well to remember the Supreme Court's potential for fallibility and the chance for correction at times like these when the court's decisions can engender intense controversy."

local.title: Legislature rejects benefit change for managers
local.summary: MAYVILLE – After a couple of months of indecision, county lawmakers have rejected a proposal to have managers get the same retirement insurance benefits as union employees. Back in September, the Chautauqua County Legislature looked at modifying a local law that would permit a retiring manager to “r
local.body:
MAYVILLE - After a couple of months of indecision, county lawmakers have rejected a proposal to have managers get the same retirement insurance benefits as union employees.

Back in September, the Chautauqua County Legislature looked at modifying a local law that would permit a retiring manager to "receive paid health insurance coverage after retirement at the rate which matches that of the highest service-related calculation afforded within any county union collective bargaining unit agreement."

At both the September and October legislature meetings, county supervisors spoke out, saying that there have been times when union employees were declining promotions simply because the union benefits were better than what they would get as a supervisor. Others said that managers had left their supervisory role to rejoin the union later in their careers, simply because of the benefits the union members get in retirement.

In both September and October, the legislature sent the change to the local law back to committee for further discussion.

During Wednesday night's county legislature meeting, Legislator Tom Nelson, D-Jamestown, said he supported the change. "First, I think it’s important to provide competitive benefits to attract and retain qualified management employees. Second, I believe we should recognize the years of service our management employees have given to the county. But mostly I support this because it protects benefits earned in union positions. Many of our county employees spent years serving the county beginning in union positions before moving into management," he said.

But Legislator Fred Johnson, R-Westfield, disagreed. "What Legislator Nelson was talking about is the heart of a good comp and benefits policy and strategy. This is not the way to go about it. ... If we have a compensation issue at any part of our employees relative to the marketplace, then let’s deal with it in a professional manner. But cherry-picking a particular benefit and then just running it across the management group is not a way to go about this," he said.

The local law as written did not specify what the potential cost would be. That bothered Legislator Chuck Nazzaro, D-Jamestown, who was sworn into office in October. "I’ve not heard the cost to the county," he said.

During various committee meetings, there had been talk about what the potential costs would be, but that was never made clear.

local.title: Shotguns, rifles, crossbows: the changing face of deer hunting
local.summary: For generations, deer hunters across Western New York headed into the woods carrying shotguns. It was simply the accepted way of hunting big game in many parts of New York State where rifle use was restricted by law. For many longtime hunters, that familiar shotgun remains their firearm of choice to
local.body:
For generations, deer hunters across Western New York headed into the woods carrying shotguns. It was simply the accepted way of hunting big game in many parts of New York State where rifle use was restricted by law.

For many longtime hunters, that familiar shotgun remains their firearm of choice today.

Why not? A dependable shotgun, properly sighted in and loaded with the right ammunition, can still be an excellent deer-hunting tool.

Since those old days, hunting regulations have evolved, and so has ammunition technology.

So, over the years, New York lawmakers gradually expanded rifle privileges for big-game hunting on a county-by-county basis. Chautauqua County joined the list in 2011, initially allowing rifle use in designated areas south of Route 20. Wyoming County’s rifle authorization, initially established in 2011, became permanent in 2013. Cattaraugus and Allegheny Counties have also long permitted rifle hunting.

Today, hunters have more choices, although restrictions remain. Rifles are not permitted for big-game hunting in Erie and Monroe counties -- but crossbows are, and certain geographic exceptions apply elsewhere. Of course, we hunters should always consult the latest NYSDEC regulations and maps before heading afield.

Traditional 12-gauge, 2 3⁄4-inch rifled slugs remain popular, but today’s hunters can choose from a wide selection of ammunition, including 3-inch (magnum) and 3 1⁄2-inch (super-magnum) shells where firearms are chambered to accept them. Sixteen- and 20-gauge options also offer effective alternatives. Deer slug types include Foster (rifled solid lead), Brenneke (hard lead alloy) -- both of these for smooth bore barrels, and Sabot (lead, copper or polymer tipped) inside a plastic sleeve engineered for rifled barrels. The newer slug designs offer improved accuracy, expansion and weight retention, depending on the firearm and ammunition combination.

Myself, I have many favorite rifles, but my favorite short distance deer hunting tool is still my Remington 1100 shotgun. I like the balance, the feel, and the total accuracy of this firearm with a saboted slug fired through the Hastings rifled barrel with a 1.5-4X Leupold scope. They call it a "tack-driver." All the slugs on a target within a half inch at 75 yards. Shotguns in WNY are a proven deer hunting tradition.

local.title: Buffalo woman charged after feds seize 27 pounds of drugs, loaded handgun
local.summary: A 48-year-old woman charged after federal investigators seized more than 27 pounds of drugs, a loaded handgun and cash from a Buffalo home.
local.body: Federal authorities charged a 48-year-old woman after seizing more than 27 pounds of drugs, a loaded handgun and cash from a Buffalo home on Thursday.Authorities say the seizure happened at 231 Comstock Avenue, where they found approximately 22 pounds of fentanyl, five pounds of cocaine and an additional quantity of methamphetamine.Keona Goins, 48, of Buffalo, is charged by federal criminal complaint with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and cocaine. The charges carry a maximum potential sentence of 20 years in prison.Neighbors describe the area as generally quiet. Trinity Dunkin, who lives in the neighborhood, said, "For the most part, it's very quiet on these streets."But federal investigators say the alleged drug activity could have had serious consequences for the community."The alleged criminal activity poisons our communities, fuels violence, endangers the vulnerable, ultimately putting lives at risk," said Anthony Patron, special agent in charge with Homeland Security Investigations.U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo said the investigation was part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, a government partnership focused on disrupting criminal organizations."This investigation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, which is a government partnership focused on eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, human smuggling and trafficking rings all operating here in the United States and abroad," DiGiacomo said.The investigation involved several federal, state and local agencies, including Homeland Security Investigations, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the FBI, Buffalo Police and the Niagara County Sheriff's Office.DiGiacomo said authorities intend to continue pursuing drug trafficking investigations."The message is very simple. If you choose to traffic narcotics in this district or this community, you will face the combined efforts of law enforcement and prosecution. It's that simple," DiGiacomo said.For Dunkin, the seizure is a relief."I'm glad they found it before it got worse," she said.DiGiacomo said federal prosecutors will continue using every lawful tool available to investigate and prosecute those accused of trafficking dangerous drugs.

local.title: SUNY enrollment grows for fourth straight year, but Buffalo State, Fredonia continue to struggle
local.summary: SUNY enrollment is up for the fourth year in a row, but some Western New York campuses aren't seeing the same growth.
local.body: Enrollment across the State University of New York (SUNY) system is growing for the fourth consecutive year, reversing a long-running trend of declining student populations. "Our four-year institutions, the tuition for a full year is $7,070. local.title: Disabled woman removed from Depew group home without proper warning, family seeks answers
local.summary: A family is outraged that their disabled loved one was removed from a group home in Depew and sent to one in Orchard Park without proper warning.
local.body: A family is outraged that their disabled loved one was removed from a group home in Depew and sent to one in Orchard Park without proper warning."We were given less than 24 hours’ notice that this was going to happen," remarked Rose Collins, sister.Laure Mercurio, 60, has a developmental disability, uses a wheelchair and is nonverbal. She relies on round-the-clock care. Unable to speak for herself, her sisters, Rose Collins and Paul Mercurio, are speaking out on her behalf. "It's unacceptable. It's unheard of," said her sister Paula Mercurio.The family got a call learning that Laure and six other medically frail residents moved out from the state-operated group home on Conway in Depew, a place they say their sister was thriving at."It's been a lovely, cohesive family unit. It's been a breath of fresh air, both for our sister, who has blossomed and thrived," Mercurio noted."This is totally unacceptable to us. They have basically ripped apart this family unit. They decimated it," Collins said.The family was told it was an emergency evacuation to remodel two bathrooms in the home. Laure was moved to a smaller group home on Baker Road in Orchard Park. But others were also sent to group homes in Perrysburg and New Albion.Normally, the Office for People with Developmental Disabilities offers families a chance to do a site visit before a move, but that never happened."Laying eyes on the particular place is hugely important — meeting the people that may be taking care of Laure is extremely important," Mercurio explained."She now doesn't have much room to ambulate in the home. It's a very smaller home," Collins noted.Staffers were also moved around, and the family worries about continuity of care."If she misses any meds for her epilepsy she can go into cluster seizures, and potentially die," Mercurio worries."Medication errors increase, and Laure is very medical frail. local.title: 'They want some answers': 77 families sue over remains removed from St. Matthew's Cemetery
local.summary: Seventy-seven families are suing St. Matthew's Cemetery, alleging it knowingly buried their loved ones on unstable ground.
local.body: Seventy-seven families whose loved ones' remains were removed from burial sites at St. Matthew's Cemetery have filed a lawsuit alleging the cemetery knew the ground where they were buried was unstable.A total of 220 burial sites were disinterred after the creek bed along Cayuga Creek began to collapse in 2019."The plaintiffs believe that St. Matthew's Cemetery should not have buried their loved ones in the section of the cemetery that they did because they were aware prior to the burials that the ground was unstable," said attorney Barry Covert, who represents the 77 families.Covert alleges the land was not properly tested for engineering purposes and that cemetery employees had warned about the condition of the ground."Even employees of the cemetery had told the cemetery that this ground was unstable, nobody should be buried there," Covert said.Covert said the families are still seeking answers about what happened and exactly where their loved ones' remains were relocated.7 News was at the cemetery in April 2019 as coffins were being moved. At the time, some family members said they did not know the work was happening until they learned about it from 7 News."It's not fair to families to have to see it live on Facebook or whatever," Tina Sanders told 7 News iCovert said the families initially tried to pursue a class-action lawsuit but have now filed this lawsuit.He said many of the people buried in the affected section came from low-income and minority families."They really feel as though their loved ones were mistreated because of that, that they were buried in a section of the cemetery that was not appropriately tested to make sure that their loved ones could be buried there," Covert said.For the families, Covert said the lawsuit is also about getting an explanation for what happened."They want some answers as to why this occurred," he said.7 News has reached out to the cemetery's owner, Buffalo City Cemetery, for a response.Join the Southtowns Community News Facebook group to connect with neighbors and learn about what's happening in your community.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. local.title: AG Letitia James sues former Rochester Holiday Inn, alleging forced labor and trafficking
local.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James is suing Nayan Patel, the former downtown Rochester Holiday Inn owner and operator; its renovation contractor Roman Petrik; and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts. James alleges forced labor and trafficking.
local.body:
State authorities claim one of the nation's largest hospitality companies overlooked human trafficking during renovations of a downtown Rochester hotel, allegedly labeling the unpaid workers "squatters" and pledging incentives if the hotel owner evicted them from the property.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is suing Nayan Patel, the former downtown Rochester Holiday Inn owner and operator; its renovation contractor Roman Petrik; and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts. The lawsuit accuses them of knowingly benefiting from what the Attorney General's Office argues was a forced labor scheme involving dozens of immigrant workers.

The lawsuit, filed in state Supreme Court, alleges workers were recruited with promises of hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but went months without pay, worked as many as 112 hours a week, and faced threats of deportation, eviction from the floor they were living on and arrest when they demanded their wages.

The allegations overlap the timeline when the former Holiday Inn on State Street downtown began taking in asylum seekers from New York City. That program brought aid workers into the hotel who learned of the problems and alerted authorities.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans said in a statement that he is appalled by the allegations.

"The City of Rochester engaged these same owners in an attempt to bring that facility up to City Code and ensure the safety of hotel guests and employees – and ultimately forced its closure due to continued concerns," Evans wrote. "We will support Attorney General James as she proceeds with this lawsuit and remain committed to working with the foreclosing mortgage holder to get this important Downtown hotel property in the hands of a new owner."

The city ordered the hotel closed in June, citing multiple fire and building code violations. The building has been tied up in foreclosure proceedings since September.

In an email to WXXI News, a spokesperson from IHG said it condemns trafficking in any form and that the company denies that they had any knowledge of serious misconduct by Patel or Petrik.

entertainment.title: Jordan Brunoli, Bassist With Australian Indie Rockers Bugs, Dies at 31
entertainment.summary: Brunoli was diagnosed with stage 4 colorectal cancer in 2025.
entertainment.body:
Jordan Brunoli, bass player with Brisbane-based indie rock trio Bugs, died on Wednesday night (Nov. 18) following a public battle with cancer. He was 31.

Brunoli was diagnosed with stage 4 colorectal cancer in 2025, and, rather than choosing the quiet life, advocated for others suffering with illness. Related Doja Cat Blasts Rockstar Games for Leaving Her Music Out of 'GTA 6': 'I'm So F--kin Bitter' Brothers Osborne & Cody Johnson Celebrate Teen Rebellion in 'Born And Raised Hell': 'It's Kind of Our Story as a Town' Eminem Takes a Trip Down Memory Lane for 'The Slim Shady Show'-Inspired Episode of Spotify's 'Billions Club' Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

The rocker performed on the band’s four albums, including their latest collection, Head Noise , which dropped Aug. 28 and was shortlisted for a J Award for Australian album of the year . The band’s previous album, 2022’s Cooties (via Community Music), crashed the top 10 of the ARIA Top 20 Vinyl Albums Chart, peaking at No. 4.

In 2020, Brunoli and his bandmates had an unexpected breakthrough with their Like A Version cover of Mallrat’s “Charlie,” which broke into the Hottest 100 the following year at No. 91, and landed at No. 25 in 2023’s Hottest 100 Like A Versions of all time poll.

Bugs presented a fundraiser for Brunoli at local venue The Tivoli last October. A slew of Brisbane’s brightest participated in the show, bearing the name Saving A Bug’s Life , including Dear Seattle, Beddy Rays, Sly Withers, Hope D, The Buoys, TOWNS, RAAVE TAPES, and others.

Following his diagnosis, Jordan was a regular on triple j’s Hack program, on which he shared updates on his health, his outlook as a young person facing a terminal diagnosis, and to remind other young Australians to look after their health.

He described music as “therapy,” and nothing was better than playing with his bandmates Connor Brooker and Brock Weston.

“Especially when I’m really down, I’ll just play guitar as much as my fingers will allow,” he told Hack in 2025. “You’ll have to break my arms and peel my entire skin off before I’ll stop playing.”

entertainment.title: Selena Gomez Shares Her Reaction to Martin Short Ruining Her Wedding Cake
entertainment.summary: The Only Murders in the Building star previously admitted to inadvertently cutting into Gomez's cake during her wedding to Benny Blanco
entertainment.body:
Martin Short and Selena Gomez stopped by Jimmy Kimmel Live to promote the new season of Only Murders in the Building , which is set in London. But before they could discuss the new episodes, Jimmy Kimmel asked Short to revisit a story he told on the late-night show in January, which involved the actor almost ruining Gomez’s wedding to Benny Blanco .

Kimmel urged Short to “summarize the story” before getting to Gomez’s perspective. “First of all, it’s insane because I am blameless in the story,” Short said. “Selena has the most fabulous, beautiful wedding imaginable. And in this one major tent where the after-ceremony took place. [There were] 18, 20 musicians and a dance floor and a nightclub.”

He recalled there being sections with sofas and chairs for groups to sit. “And there was this cake there,” he said. “And I just assumed it was a cake for each individual [group]. It turned out to be the wedding cake.” Short, who admitted to “maybe” having had a drink, cut into the cake with a fork as Steve Martin was leaving the party. Kimmel then revealed a photo of the mutilated cake.

“I love the teeth marks of the fork where he tried to save it,” Gomez said. “Really nicely done.”

Gomez added that Short “apparently insisted” that no one tell her what had happened. “They managed to put it together,” she said. “And I didn’t care. I was there, but I didn’t know what happened. And then all of a sudden, somebody comes up and they’re like, ‘Marty cut your cake. And I think he was eating it.’ I was like, ‘Oh!’ So I run and he looks like a little dog with his tail between his legs. I go, ‘I heard you ate my cake.'”

entertainment.title: U2 Ride to No. 1 on ARIA Chart With ‘Carnaval De Luz’
entertainment.summary: Jamie Miller becomes for the first male solo artist to top the national singles chart in almost 18 months, with "Babydoll."
entertainment.body:
U2 ’s Carnaval De Luz (via Island/Universal) enjoys the brightest possible start on the Australia’s albums chart , as it opens at No. 1.

With that fast opening, Carnaval De Luz becomes the Irish rock legends’ 12th chart leader in these parts. The Rock And Roll Hall of Fame inductees bagged their first No. 1 album with The Unforgettable Fire in 1984, a year after the ARIA Charts launched, and kept the hits coming with Rattle and Hum (1988), Achtung Baby (1991), Zooropa (1993), Pop (1997), The Best Of 1980-1990 (1998), All That You Can’t Leave Behind (2000), The Best Of 1990-2000 (2002), How To Dismantle An Atomic Bomb (2004), U218 Singles (2006), and No Line On The Horizon (2009).

According to ARIA, U2’s dozen No. 1s places the foursome equal fourth on the all-time leaderboard, tied with Madonna, and behind only The Beatles and Taylor Swift (14 each) and leader Jimmy Barnes with 16. Including Cold Chisel recordings, Barnes has 22 ARIA No. 1s. The latest ARIA Chart, published Friday, Nov. 20, is something of a birthday party for a bunch of veteran acts. Those celebrating include Aphex Twin , whose 25 th anniversary edition of Drukqs (Warp/Inertia) drops in at No. 14, for the British electronic music great’s highest-charting album, bettering the No. 45 for Selected Ambient Works Volume II .

Also, the late king of pop, Michael Jackson , returns to the chart at No. 21 with his former leader, Invincible , following its 25 th anniversary release. And Australian punk rock act Trophy Eyes bounces in at No. 24 with 10 th anniversary edition of Chemical Miracle .

The latest frame welcomes new releases from German DJ and production duo DJ Heartstring (No. 17 with Sentimental Ultra via Steel City Dance Discs), Sydney pub rockers The Johnnys (No. 40 with Rarehide – Outtakes, B-sides And Rarities via Cheersquad Records & Tapes) and Queensland sibling act Vixens of Fall (No. 48 with the independently-released Fox Hollow ).

Over on the ARIA Singles Chart , Welsh pop artist Jamie Miller is crowned as “Babydoll” (Universal) rises 4-1. The former Voice U.K. contestant becomes not just the first artist to hit No. 1 in 2026 with his first charted single, he’s the only solo male artist to top the singles tally this year. The last time a solo male artist led the ARIA Chart was Justin Bieber, back in July 2025 with “Daisies.”

entertainment.summary: When asked by Andy Cohen if she was able to snag the iconic prop her character Katniss Everdeen used in the films, the actress realized on-air she may have "lost it, or I guess it was stolen."
entertainment.body:
Jennifer Lawrence thinks a bow and arrow she received after appearing on The Hunger Games may have been stolen from her.

The Oscar winner appeared on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen on Thursday night alongside Josh Hutcherson , marking their first joint interview in over 10 years. The appearance was tied to the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping , the prequel film where they reprise their respective roles of Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

Andy Cohen questioned them about a number of Hunger Games -related topics, including if they agree that Catching Fire is the best movie in the franchise (Lawrence agreed, while Hutcherson said the first Hunger Games is his favorite) and their first impressions of each other when they first met to work on the film. Cohen asked Lawrence if she was able to obtain one of her character’s famed bow and arrows, which led her to a realization. “I think I lost it, or I guess it was stolen,” Lawrence said, dumbfounded. “Where am I going to lose it?”

entertainment.title: ‘Spin City’ actor Richard Kind reveals ‘horrible’ decades-long struggle with mysterious health condition
entertainment.summary: The Trenton, NJ-born star admitted he still struggles to accept the condition.
entertainment.body:
Actor Richard Kind has revealed he’s been struggling with a mysterious health condition for decades.

The “Spin City” star, 69, opened up about living with the skin condition vitiligo, saying that he had tan skin until around age 34, but then white patches started to appear on his body.

“I have it all over my body,” Kind said during Tuesday’s episode of Michael Rosenbaum’s “Inside of You” podcast .

“I don’t know how I got it. Could have been nerves. I could have caught a virus. I don’t know what it was,” he added.

The Trenton, NJ-born actor, who played Paul Lassiter on “Spin City” from 1996 to 2002, recalled that he noticed changes to his skin after a vacation at Club Med.

“I came back and all of a sudden, I started getting a white spot here, and then a white spot here, and it’d come on my hands, and then I could get a scratch, and the pigment would go,” he explained.

Vitiligo is a condition that causes patches of skin to lose their color, according to the Mayo Clinic . The affected areas can grow over time and appear anywhere on the body.

Kind admitted he still struggles to accept the condition, both physically and mentally.

entertainment.title: ‘Sh*t Happens’ Is Full of Dark Humor, But Its Director Knows It Will Cause a Stink in the DR
entertainment.summary: José María Cabral, who has seen three of his films submitted for the Oscars, just premiered his new feature at Tallinn – and there is more to it than it might seem to folks outside his home country.
entertainment.body:
José María Cabral has seen three of his films submitted for the best international feature film Oscar race by the Dominican Republic, namely The Projectionist , Woodpeckers , and Checkmate . That means that you can probably trust his gut when it comes to picking themes that are cinematic and feature more than a trickle of ideas. So, why did he just celebrate the world premiere of his newest film that is not only a black comedy but also has the ominous title Sh*t Happens ? Cue the toilet humor, you say? Well, let’s first flush away any doubt you may have that this writer just made all this stuff up. The film did indeed premiere Thursday night in the Official Competition of the 30th edition of Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF). And here is what it is about: The young daughter of a wealthy couple suffers from gut issues that the doctors just can’t seem to heal. The young nanny Lidi, portrayed by Cindy Galán, remains her upbeat self though, making the little girl smile despite all the health worries. And maid Dominga (Isabel Spencer) handles cooking and cleaning, sharing a small bunk bed with Lidi. Gracie Abrams ’ Daughter from Hell is now, well, more hell-ish.

The Grammy nominated singer and songwriter today (Nov. 20) drops the deluxe edition of Daughter from Hell , an expanded version that now features five fresh cuts.

Daughter from Hell (Deluxe) collects newbies “Out of Nowhere,” which became a fan fave after Abrams debuted it during her 2025 Glastonbury Festival spot (where Paul McCartney was watching on from the sidelines); and “Crazy Girl,” which appeared on the vinyl exclusive and is now available digitally for the first time. Other bonus tracks into the previously revealed “Here You Come, There You Go,” produced by Jim-E Stack and co-written with Amy Allen; “Love Letter;” and “Lost It In.” Explore Gracie Abrams See latest videos, charts and news

Was she a beastly kid? Not exactly, just a “defiant person,” which can be “turbulent” for mom and dad (the film director J.J. Abrams). “This is a thank-you note to her.”
